945670cf35c6.name: MT | Research Notes
945670cf35c6.text:
Nvidia lost about $2.7 trillion in 45 days, more than the whole crypto market is worth!

Since its Oct 6 record, the stock is down nearly half, to $125.53 on Nov 20. In the middle of it, Nvidia posted the biggest quarter in its history. Investors stopped asking how much it sells and started asking who is in charge and what is in the books.

> Oct 6: a record high near $243, a market value of about $5.7 trillion.

> Oct 22 to Nov 5: the first fear was who pays for AI. Shares fell about 4% on Oct 22 and again on Oct 30, then 9% on Nov 5. Analysts pointed at Nvidia backing customers who buy its chips (circular financing).

> Nov 12: CEO Jensen Huang resigned after a board probe into reports about his private life. The stock opened about 13% lower. CFO Colette Kress became interim CEO.

> Nov 17: sales of $115.8 billion, up 103%, and a $130 billion forecast. The same day, the Wall Street Journal reported an SEC probe into whether Nvidia's disclosures misled investors.

> Nov 18: the stock fell 2.9% after the chairman said Huang will not return and no successor was named.

> Nov 20: Reuters reported SEC staff are examining potential accounting issues. Shares fell 14%, a record one-week loss of about $900 billion and the worst week since 2008. Open questions: Singapore, which booked about $104 billion of 2025 sales (Financial Times), and customers paying slower. An investigation is not an accusation.

What 45 days of Nvidia candles showed?
- Record numbers do not stop a sale once the question changes
- Fear stacked on fear, each headline hitting a stock already down
- A probe is a question, and the price trades it before any answer

Great numbers, shaky trust, which one moves the price more?

Experience, not financial advice.
945670cf35c6.note: Context on the drawdown: ~$2.7T of market cap lost in 45 days before today's rebound.

CRWD.name: AGTP
CRWD.text:
CrowdStrike just agreed to buy Zscaler for $43.9B. Here's what you need to know.

The rumor from Friday is now official. CrowdStrike $CRWD announced Monday that it will acquire Zscaler $ZS in an all-stock deal, with no cash involved. The announcement came alongside CrowdStrike's quarterly results.

This is the largest cybersecurity acquisition in history. It tops Google's $32B purchase of Wiz.

Zscaler holders get 1.135 CrowdStrike shares for each Zscaler share. That works out to about $260.41 per share, a 34% premium to Friday's close.

The pitch is network security. The deal brings Zscaler's network security and Zero Trust tech into CrowdStrike's Falcon platform. CrowdStrike says it adds over $185B to its addressable market. It also opens cross-selling to roughly 8,000 Zscaler customers.

The deal still needs Zscaler shareholder approval and regulatory approval. It is expected to close in the second half of CrowdStrike's fiscal 2028.

Shares fell on the news. CrowdStrike was at $229.44, down 5.76%. Zscaler was at $194.82, down 5.29%. Some investors have criticized paying with CrowdStrike's richly valued stock, while others call it a smart use of expensive equity to buy a fast-growing rival.

CrowdStrike also reported Q3 fiscal 2027 results.

Key numbers:
- Deal value: $43.9B, all stock
- Exchange ratio: 1.135 CRWD shares per ZS share
- Implied price: $260.41, a 34% premium
- Combined annual recurring revenue: over $10B
- Added addressable market: over $185B
- Q3 revenue: $1.58B vs $1.53B expected, up 28% YoY
- Q3 adjusted EPS: $0.34 vs $0.31 expected
- Ending ARR: $6.26B, up 27%
- Net new ARR: $419.2M, up 58%
- FY27 revenue guide raised to $6.078B-$6.084B, vs $6B expected

CrowdStrike has gone from talks to a signed deal, with closing set for the second half of fiscal 2028.
CRWD.note: Explainer: rumor became a definitive $43.9B all-stock deal, announced with CrowdStrike's Q3 print.

CRWD.name: ξth.c

CRWD.note: Deal mechanics: a fixed 1.135 exchange ratio means the deal value floats with CRWD's stock.

5 TMT takeaways from last week:

1/ The Nasdaq 100 fell 10.4%, its worst week since March 2020. Semis lost ~17%, and the S&P 500 dropped 8.6%, ending roughly 12% below its October high after seven consecutive down sessions. Tech has seen aggressive rotation for six months, but Friday felt different, perhaps the first session that smelled like panic. The VIX touched 40 before cooling to around 36 late in the session. Some of the volatility bid appeared exhausted into the close, which could help a temporary bounce. But strong $NVDA results and a massive Anthropic IPO failed to restore confidence. Investors are questioning who finances the next round of AI spending, what returns it earns and whether earnings estimates hold. With the 10-year near 5% and further Fed tightening in focus, selling spread beyond AI into broader growth concerns. The market feels increasingly bear-ish, even without a formal 20% index drawdown.

2/ $NVDA doubled revenue to $115.8B and guided the next quarter to $130B. Demand was not the weak point. The CEO search, a 10-Q still to come and reports of an SEC accounting investigation left other questions open. The board also faces a difficult appointment: if the investigation establishes wrongdoing, an internal successor could leave doubts about whether enough has changed. If it does not, refusing to reconsider Jensen would be a mistake. I think the stock could remain in the penalty box under either scenario, despite strong operating results. For the stock to get back to grace, and perhpas even the market, Jensen getting re-instated seems to be the right path.

3/ $ANT public offering reached $93.5B gross, including secondary shares, alongside a $26B private placement. Even that failed to settle the funding debate. Consensus forecasts put cloud provider cash burn at ~$361B in 2027, versus ~$140B this year. Nvidia is also becoming more selective about customer financing commitments. Capital remains available, but its cost and conditions matter more. I would distinguish projects with secured financing, tenants and power from those still depending on all three coming together.

4/ Positioning and thin liquidity amplified the move. Single stock shorting was the heaviest since June 2022, ETF shorts rose 11%, and market depth was near the year’s low. That helps explain the speed of the decline. It does not prove everyone has sold: systematic exposure was low, but broader positioning remained above average. Friday showed signs of panic; I am less convinced we have seen enough selling across investor groups to call a durable bottom.

5/ $PANW was a standout, as I discussed in a separate post: $630M of net new next-generation security ARR and a higher full-year outlook. $KEYS  orders rose 53%, while Lenovo’s GPU-server revenue grew more than 300%. There is no uniform collapse in operating demand. My concern is that financing costs, lower project returns and approval delays eventually change future spending plans. The selloff may not be over; sideways trading is also possible. Beyond a temporary bounce, I still do not see enough catalysts for a meaningful, sustained rally. I would keep the hedges on and add selectively.

#TMT #AI #Semiconductors

MU.name: Semiconductor Insider
MU.text:
Korean memory stocks are bouncing hard after Jensen Huang’s return.

Samsung Electronics jumped about 7% and SK Hynix rose over 8% in early trading. The move follows a sharp rebound in the US overnight, where NVIDIA soared more than 31% after the board brought Huang back as CEO.
MU.note: Memory peers Samsung and SK Hynix rallied 7-8% too, a read-through for MU.
